The load failure of a `ZZ32Vector` as a generic's type argument (the size-cost entry above, "no ledger row yet") is the descriptor class's name: both classes call it `RTTIv` (`FZZ32Vector.java:79-82`) while stamped code asks for `<class>$RTTIc` (`runtimeSystem/MethodInstantiater.java:134-138`), and a probe-only copy with an `RTTIc` alias runs (`probes/rttic-alias.patch`, `out-VecGeneric-rttic.txt`). A native helper cannot take a Java array: the wrapper generator skips every method with an array parameter (`compiler/nativeInterface/SignatureParser.java:45-55`). Written by Christine Flood (`f4973a717`, `24717d4ad`, 2011) and extended by Guy Steele (`d535963cb`, 2011-10-12).
119	- **A generic object referenced without its static arguments is a static error on the compiled path, and the checker never consults the expected type for it** (2026-09-19, `explorations/compiler-probes/maybe-inference/inference.md`): `b: Box[\ZZ32\] = Box` fails with `Ill-formed type: Box`; a bare `Empty` as a call argument or a field default fails with `T is not in the kind env`, an internal `bug()` from `TypeAnalyzer.scala:766` reported at the declaration's span; the same forms with the static argument written compile and run on both paths. The decision is in the checker's `SVarRef` case, `typechecker/impls/Misc.scala:624-641`, whose `:639-640` keeps the uninstantiated type under the team's own `TODO: handle missing static args`; static-argument inference exists only for arrows (`STypesUtil.scala:912-930`, called from application and coercion), and a parametric empty case reached by `coerce` still fails bare. Under `walk` the same forms are `InterpreterBug: Couldn't figure out Empty[\T\](uninstantiated) <: Opt[\ZZ32\]`. Consequence for row 331: a parametric `Nothing[\T\]` would serve the corpus's `Nothing[\ZZ32\]` and never the specification's bare `= Nothing`; the non-parametric object plus `coerce` that the prelude uses is the only shape that compiles, so `Maybe` stays as landed. Incidental: `typecase` over a user-declared generic object crashes code generation (`Error trying to close method scope`, `CodeGen.java:2802`), row 340. Corrected the same day by the minimal reproducer (`compiler-probes/maybe-inference/probes/TcPlain.fss`): neither the generic object nor `typecase` alone is the trigger; a `typecase` used directly as a function or method body whose value needs an implicit coercion (`IntLiteral` to a declared `ZZ32`) makes ASM's stack-map frame computation fail (`ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` under `MethodWriter.visitMaxs`, relabelled by the `catch (Throwable)` at `CodeGen.java:2801-2802`); wrapped in `do … end` the same body compiles, and every gated use of the shape returns `()` so never reaches the coercion.
120	- The gate: two corpora, hand-ported, sharing no file name; only `parser_tests/` is read by both; no test compares the paths on one program; interpreter tests pass on "no exception and no `fail` in output" (`FileTests.java:367-371`), compiler run tests on exit code plus `PASS`. `fortress.unittests.noopt=true` (`default_repository/configuration:51`) hides 226 tests and leaves the 43-file bytecode optimizer with zero. Every `testSystem` shard runs `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` (`build.xml:1184`), so no gated test sees concurrency; `TransactionJUTest`'s multi-threaded half is commented out (`TestTask.java:43-44`). No `nat`-parameterised program is compiled or run; the cache round trip is not asserted (`ASTJUTest.java:654`). 121 `.fss` inside green directories are dark; `linker_tests`, `compiler_regressions`, `BirdyLib`, the `not_working_*` directories are orphaned (`map/test-coverage.md`).
121	
122	## The container
123	
124	- The process cost of the climbs and the batches — the eight-rung climb's wall clock and its gate share, the limits of parallelism on this box, and each batch's agents, tokens, tool calls and span — is measured in `explorations/coordinator/iteration-cost.md`, `coordinator/repair-batch-review.md` and the batch records; the conclusions it produced are in `POSITIONS.md` and in `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`, and the entries themselves are in `FACTS-history.md`.
125	- The Bash tool's 10-minute ceiling kills long runs; check runs go under the `Monitor` tool (1800000 ms), sequential, nothing else running when a number is to be kept.
126	- The disk allowance fills with parser-generation temp directories: every run that imports a grammar generates a Rats! parser into a fresh `/tmp/fortress<random>rats` directory (`RatsUtil.getTempDir`, `syntax_abstractions/rats/RatsUtil.java:138-146`, via `IOUtil.createAndMarkTempDirectory`), 5.8 MB each, never deleted; 723 of them (4.2 GB) filled the allowance on 2026-09-15 and broke a worker's tool output mid-run ("no space left on device"). Deficit until fixed at the source (an edit under the sealed tree, or a `deleteOnExit`); mitigation in our tree: `explorations/experiment/env.sh` removes them when sourced, and `df` must be checked before any long run.
127	- The Bash tool's 10-minute ceiling; `Monitor` for long runs (the microGPT-runs entry above).
128	- A container can be lost outright: the coordinating session of 2026-09-17 (`bdff267d-…`) died mid-workflow and could not be re-provisioned, because the branch it was created from was no longer found on the remote. Recovery moved into the blinded run's container, which already had the checkout and toolchain. Cost: four workflow agents (~798k tokens), their worktrees, and the 13 hours after the last transcript snapshot at 20:31. Everything through `2ab1d6d8` was pushed and safe, and `REPAIR-BATCH.md` kept the batch runnable. Mechanism, the three traps and the recovery procedure: `explorations/coordinator/remote-container.md`.
129	- The transcript backup fires on the main session's Stop, not on any agent's completion, and swallows all errors: a session inside one long turn is not being backed up and a failed push is silent. Workflow-agent transcripts were outside its globs until 2026-09-18; oversized transcripts now split at 64 MiB, and the wrapper packs loose objects because the clone ships `gc.auto=0`.
130	- **The Workflow harness runs two agents at once on this box** (measured 2026-09-18, four one-command agents in one `parallel()`: agents 0 and 1 started 19:14:08, agents 2 and 3 at 19:14:31 after the first pair finished at 19:14:23; `batched-climb-plan.md` §2). `model: 'opus'` in `agent()` resolves to a fixed model identifier, readable in each agent transcript's `message.model` field and not written here (protocol §4); an agent with no `model` inherits the session's. A subagent's floor is about 45k tokens before it does anything (183k for the four). Prompt caching across parallel agents covers the system prompt and tools only (33,022 tokens read by agents 1–3) and not the first user message (11,010 written by each), because a cache read lands only at a breakpoint the harness placed and a shared prefix inside one message is not one.
131	- The VM can be restarted under a live session with the disk intact: 2026-09-18 23:22 UTC, 25 minutes into the repair batch's re-run, kernel build string fc-v33 → fc-v37, one JVM running (16 GB, no swap, 4 CPUs: not a memory death). Worktrees, uncommitted edits and agent transcripts survived; the Workflow run and its agents did not, and a run is relaunched, never resumed; the `wip/` branches held every pushed milestone (`remote-container.md` § The 2026-09-18 restart).
132	- **A user interrupt of the coordinating session's turn kills a background Workflow run** (2026-09-19): climb batch 1's first run, `wf_a29fd04b-a9a`, launched 07:15 UTC, lost both its rung agents at 07:46:42, the second Pavol's interrupt cut the turn that a check-in trigger had just started; both agent transcripts end at that timestamp mid-work, no result line reached the journal, and the harness no longer knew the task. The Agent tool's workers are not affected (the review worker launched after the interrupt ran to completion). The `wip/` branches held F's three and M's three milestones and M's worktree its uncommitted report, so the relaunch at 08:25 from the same base continued under the prefix's continuation clause. Cost: about 40 minutes of two workers. Rule: while a Workflow runs, a check-in must not be interrupted mid-turn; and a batch is relaunched, never resumed, after any such death.
133	- **A manual compaction issued between turns leaves a running Workflow alive** (found 2026-09-19 by a worker in the archived transcript of session `bdff267d`, `transcripts` branch, parts file `001.jsonl`): the eight-rung climb's run `wf_73833dfb-d25` (launched 2026-09-17 06:00:57 UTC) survived two `/compact` commands, boundaries 10:47:33 (442,504 tokens before, 130 s) and 14:25:25 (177,831 tokens, 153 s), both typed while the session sat between turns; rung 5's commit landed 84 s after the first boundary, rungs 6-8 and the final re-run followed, and the run's completion notification arrived 14:39:09 with all eight rungs. This container's three compactions (09-18 18:38, 22:54; 09-19 06:38) coincided with no run. So the rule is: compact between turns, never send during a turn; the 09-19 death was a mid-turn interrupt, not a compaction. Caveat: that run's journal and agent transcripts are not in the backup, so the agents' survival is inferred from their commits and the session's own status turns.
134	- **`explorations/experiment/env.sh` is the one script every probe and gate runner sources, and it is verified from its new home** (2026-09-24, after `7bc8177a3` moved `experiment/` under `explorations/`): it derives `FORTRESS_HOME` from its own location two levels up, and re-running the two shadow experiments that source it, `reviews/mie-probes/forest/forest-run.sh` (423 s) and `perf-probes/nat/runtime/run-all.sh` (669 s), reproduced every committed count and probe output (`checker-count.txt`'s six counts, stock 103 and forest 37 among them, and captures r1-r5 byte-identical); the only differences were dates, timings and line numbers shifted by the library commits `c2b4e2c95` and `d6faad28f` made after the captures. astra's scripts keep their own `experiment/` paths, which name astra's tree.
135	
136	## The ledger
137	
138	- Rows are never renumbered or moved, and the reports cite them by number; the counts by kind are derived by script in the ledger's counts (`fortress-gap-ledger.md:732`), and the revival worklist (46 items, `fortress-gap-ledger.md:592`) and `apl/lessons.md` are the two derived views. Five cost rows sit in section 15; whether they get a section of their own is Pavol's call.

explorations/compile-ladder/rung-walk-overflow/JUDGE.md:130:## 7. Decisions taken here under a silent specification

**Case by case.** Each case says what the code means, what it becomes under the principle, and the alternative from section 1 with its cost.

- **(a) The range split's `split-1`**, six sites: `Library/RangeInternals.fss:1031`, `:1046`, `:1201`, `:1221`, `:1242`, `:1266`. Row 403 and rung O's report list five; `:1266`, the loop's negative-stride branch, has the same text (by reading). It means a bit mask (section 2). It becomes `hi BITAND (BITNOT (split DOTMINUS 1))`: the same value as today, and no cost. Alternative: say "split at zero" in words, `if lo < 0 AND 0 <= hi then 0 else hi BITAND (BITNOT (split - 1)) end` (written with the element type's own zero in the generic code), which costs a comparison per split and changes Maessen's text more. A third, the compiled library's midpoint split through `floorAverage` (section 6), never overflows but moves every split point off the power-of-two boundaries Maessen chose, so it is a redesign, not a repair.
- **(b) The range split's `(lo BITXOR hi)+1`**, the same six sites. It overflows only when `lo BITXOR hi` is the maximum, for instance on a range `0:2147483647` (by reading), and `partitionL` then subtracts the 1 again inside Java, so the pair computes the highest set bit of `lo BITXOR hi`. It becomes `(lo BITXOR hi) DOTPLUS 1`, exact at no cost. Alternative: a primitive that gives the highest set bit directly, the specification's `leftmostOneBit` (`binary.tex:1289`, `:1464`), which removes the `+1`; that is a new native no site needs.
- **(c) The strided distance `(…) - lo - 1`**, four sites: `:1201`, `:1221`, `:1242`, `:1266`. It means an ordinary distance, and that distance fits whenever `mid > lo`, which always holds, but its first step `mid - lo` overflows when `lo` is the minimum and `mid` is 0 (by reading, row 403). This is must-avoid, not means-to-wrap: reorder it as `(mid - 1) - lo`, with `mid` named first, and keep the checked operators.
- **(d) `LinearCongruential`**, `Library/Random.fss:235` (measured) and `:241` (by reading). It means arithmetic modulo 2^48, done through arithmetic modulo 2^64. It becomes `((mult DOTTIMES widen(state)) DOTPLUS add) MOD modulus`: the same values, no cost, `MOD` bringing a negative wrapped value back into range as it does today. This is right only because 2^48 divides 2^64. The object is generic in its modulus (`Random.fss:222`) and built once, with 2^48 (`:253`); for a modulus that is not a power of two, today's code and this one both give wrong numbers without a word (section 11). Alternatives: exact through `ZZ`, right for every modulus, at a `BigInteger` per random number (`QuickCheckTest` alone meets 146K overflowing products); or the Mersenne twister's habit (way 1), splitting the state into 24-bit halves so every product fits, about five lines and three multiplications.
- **(e) `ChunkedSparseArray.secondaryIndex`**, `Library/ChunkedSparseArray.fss:76` (measured). It means the bits below the mask. It becomes `popCount((mask DOTMINUS 1) BITAND fe)`. Alternatives: `if mask < 0 then BITNOT mask else mask - 1 end`, or, from the bit index `indexAndMask` already computes (`:75`), `BITNOT (widen(-1) LSHIFT b)` (way 4).
- **(f) `IntMap.keySplit`**, `Library/IntMap.fss:675-676`: the negation at `:676` measured (27 `Long$Negate`), `mn-1` at `:675` by reading when the smaller key is the minimum. Both are bit masks. They become `p = partitionL(((mn DOTMINUS 1) BITXOR mx) DOTPLUS 1)` and `(DOTMINUS p) BITAND mx`. Alternative: a sign case, since the negated `p` is the minimum exactly when the keys straddle zero, where the answer is 0.
- **(g) `HeapTest`'s `spread`**, `ProjectFortress/tests/HeapTest.fss:95-99`. It means a scramble modulo 2^32: with `c1` odd, `n ↦ c1 n + c2` maps `ZZ32` onto itself one to one, so the test's keys stay distinct. It becomes `((c1 DOTTIMES n) DOTPLUS c2, n)`. Alternative: `narrow(widen(c1) widen(n) + widen(c2))` (way 2), which never overflows and gives the same value.
- **(h) `intPrim.fss:21-22` and `longPrim.fss:21-22`.** They assert of `+` and `-` exactly what the specification refuses; their author's intent (section 8) was "the boundary behaves as it should". Under the specification the wrap identity belongs to the wrapping operators and the plain ones throw, so each file asserts both: `a.minimum DOTMINUS 1 = a.maximum` and `a.maximum DOTPLUS 1 = a.minimum`, and, with a copy of rung I's helper, `overflows(fn () => a.minimum - 1)` and `overflows(fn () => a.maximum + 1)`. `longPrim`'s `a: ZZ64 = 0` holds a `ZZ32` (row 146), so all four test 32 bits there until `a` is set with `widen(0)`; that is row 146's correction, not this one's.
- **(i) The associativity properties**, `QuickCheckTest.fss:89-90` and `ReflectiveQuickCheckTest.fss:16-17`: "associativity of `+` operator over `ZZ32` domain: should pass", set against `RR64`'s "may fail". Under checked `+` associativity is not a total property of `ZZ32` (section 2). The ring the specification declares for it is ∔, so the property becomes `(p DOTPLUS q) DOTPLUS r = p DOTPLUS (q DOTPLUS r)` and still should pass. Alternatives: keep `+` and state the property only where it answers, "`+` agrees with ℤ wherever it answers", with `==>` over the sums computed in `ZZ` or with the generator held to its levels 0-2 (way 11); or move the property to `ZZ`.

**One thing all cases share.** A `ZZ64` variable that holds a `ZZ32` value (row 146) wraps at 32 bits under ∔ exactly as it does under `+` today; the respelling keeps today's values, that quirk included. Fixing row 146 is its own row.

## 10. The options as they would be put to Pavol

**Option 1, the specification's own way.** Declare ∔, ∸ (unary and binary) and ⨰ in the interpreter's library, on `Integral[\I\]` and on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64` and `ZZ`; rewrite the sites of section 9 with them; reorder the strided distance; then land rung O.
- *What the work does.* Under `walk` the new operators are bound to wrapping natives: on `NN32` and `NN64` to the natives `+` uses today, unchanged; on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` to new small wrapping classes, because rung O's patch turns today's classes into checked ones (four a width: add, subtract, multiply, negate); on `ZZ` to the exact ones, as the specification says.
- *What it produces.* Every site gives the value it gives today, because the wrapping operator is the arithmetic the site gets today. So rung O's count is expected to fall to zero. That has to be measured with the same runner, not assumed.
- *What it touches.* `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `.fss` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi` and `.fss` (for `NN32`), about 50 lines; `Int.java` and `Long.java`, eight small classes; `RangeInternals.fss` (about 16 lines at the six sites), `Random.fss` (2), `ChunkedSparseArray.fss` (1), `IntMap.fss` (2); five tests (about 12 lines). All are edits to the original tree and are flagged as such. It adds one gated test of ∔, ∸ and ⨰ at both widths' boundaries, and the rung declares its checker count, since `Integral` gains declarations.
- *What it commits him to.* Row 348 is decided for the specification's spelling in the one library. The compiled prelude's reversed operators leave with the prelude at the switch-over, and the compiled tests that use them are respelled then: 10 files, 138 matching lines (`Integer3`, `Integer4`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `AverageTest` and `ShiftTest2` in `library_tests/`; `IntegerLiteralsFolding`, `IntSemanticsRungB` and `XXXBoxDotSpellingsRungW` in `compiler_tests/`), with `BOXCROSS` becoming ⨰. The saturating family stays undeclared in the one library until a step of its own. It shares `FortressLibrary.fsi`/`.fss` with the tower-flattening rung, so the manifest orders the two.
- *Variant 1b.* The three bit-mask cases (a), (e) and (f) written with explicit sign cases instead of ∸, and the wrapping operators kept for the generator, the hash and the tests. The commitments are the same; there is more text to review, and "split at zero" is said in words.

**Option 2, restructure everything and declare no operator.** Every site is rewritten in the library's avoid-overflow habits: the zero case in the split, a highest-set-bit primitive or a guard for the `+1`, masks by shift, a sign case in `IntMap`, the hash through `widen` and `narrow`, the generator exact through `ZZ` or by split multiplication, and the tests asserting the throw, with the properties restated on the range where `+` answers.
- *What it commits him to.* No new operator, and row 348 stays open. After the switch-over the one library has no spelling for a wrap at all, so the team's compiled tests that wrap with `BOXCROSS` and `BOXPLUS` lose their operator. Each site's reasoning changes, not just its spelling. The generator costs either a `BigInteger` per random number or a five-line split multiplication. The two QuickCheck tests test different properties from today's. Under his principle, the hardware behaviour is left without its explicit spelling.

**Option 3, the whole family now.** Option 1, plus the saturating operators ⊞, ⊟, ⊡ and ⊠ in the same rung (new clamping natives under `walk`, about eight small classes).
- *What it commits him to.* The same as option 1, plus declarations that no site uses yet, and a gated test for both families. The protocol's "one variable per step" argues for doing it later.

**Not an option.** Keeping `walk` wrapping would reverse row 379, and the compiled path throws on these same bodies at the switch-over anyway (row 403).

**Recommendation (my reading, not a decision):** option 1: declare ∔, ∸ and ⨰ in the one library, respell the wrap-reliant sites and tests with them, and reorder the strided distance, as the step before rung O; the saturating family gets a later step of its own.

## 11. Found on the way

- **A sixth split site.** `Library/RangeInternals.fss:1265-1266` has the same `split-1` and the same distance as the five that row 403 and rung O's report list (by reading).
- **The unsigned types wrap under `walk` and row 379 does not cover them.** `NN32` and `NN64` arithmetic goes through `com.naturalbridge.misc.Unsigned.add`, `subtract` and `multiplyTo…`, which are bare `iadd` and `lmul` (read with `javap`; `NN32.java:103-124`, `UnsignedLong.java:104-125`), while the compiled path's `NN32` `+` throws (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:768`). Steele's gated `ProjectFortress/tests/UnsignedTest.fss:195-211` (`dc41d5000`, 2008-07-21) uses unary `-` on an unsigned value as 2^w minus that value. It is the same question as this note's, larger, and it comes later, when the unsigned natives are checked.
- **`LinearCongruential` is wrong for most moduli.** The object is generic in its modulus, but wrapping modulo 2^64 and then taking `MOD modulus` is right only when the modulus is a power of two; the library builds it only with 2^48 (`Library/Random.fss:222`, `:253`).
- **A wrapping operator under `walk` needs natives of its own.** Rung O's patch changes today's ten natives in place (`REPORT.md` § 3), so after it no native wraps; a wrapping operator bound to the old names would start to throw.
- **The box family means "toward zero" on both kinds of number.** Saturation clamps toward zero, and the same boxed operators on floats round toward zero (`opr-overview.tex:181`, `:214`). That is a design reason behind the specification's pairing, relevant to row 348.

### 9. The options, as they would be put to Pavol

1. **The specification's own way, layered as in 1.0 and 2009.**
   - Edit the normative sentences in place.
   - At each changed passage, a labelled callout that prints in both builds: a new macro,
     not `\note`, so it is not taken for the authors' remarks.
   - In Appendix I, a new section, "Changes made by the 2026 revival to the working draft",
     one entry per change. Each entry has C++'s four fields (affected section, change,
     rationale, effect) and two more: the original text, quoted verbatim with its path and
     line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, and the alternative not taken (route C), with what
     reversing to it would take.
   - One paragraph in the front-matter figure (`preamble.tex`), and a changed title-page
     line.
   - The full reasoning in a repository document, cited by the entry.
   - Optionally, route C as an entry in Proposed Features, next to the team's own note at
     `internal-document.tex:363`.

   It commits him to: one small macro; an appendix that must be kept up to date with every
   later revival change (the one place the team let decay); one repository document per
   decision; and a PDF rebuild, which every form needs anyway.

2. **Steele's CLtL2 way.** Keep the original sentences in place, marked as outdated by a
   dotted margin rule. Print the new sentences with a solid rule and a paragraph "The revival
   decided on 2026-09-24 to ...". Number each decision into an index at the end, and explain
   the convention in the front matter. It commits him to: the `changebar` package, untested
   with this document; a PDF that prints both wordings; readers who must learn the
   convention; and keeping both wordings coherent under later edits. In exchange, the original
   stays visible in place and reversing to route C is a swap of the rules.

3. **The Ada way.** One source, two PDFs: a clean normative build, and an annotated build with
   inserted and deleted text marked and a reason beside each change. It commits him to:
   reworking the release switch (today it also hides the implementation-status boxes), a first
   release build, and two committed PDFs to keep in step.

4. **Keep the history outside, the Java and Python way.** Edit in place with no mark in the
   PDF. The original text, reasoning and route C go in a repository document and the commit
   message, and the frozen copy holds the original wording. It commits him to nothing in the
   build, and to a PDF that cannot tell its reader that a rule changed or why.

What decides between them is how much of D2, D4 and D5 must be readable in the PDF itself,
without the repository. Options 1 and 2 carry all three in the PDF, option 3 carries them in
the second PDF, and option 4 carries none. Between 1 and 2 the choice is whether the original
wording should sit in the appendix (quoted once, in the entry) or in the body (printed beside
the new rule).

My reading, not a decision: option 1. It is the specification's own form (its empty Appendix I

### 2.6 Where the two differ, and the worker's reading

Read from the code, not measured:

- **A size made at run time.** `array[E](n)` and `reflect` on the compiled path wait on the array review's decision D (design brief § 12).
  - Under (b) such a size's descriptor is `RTTIsize.of(String.valueOf(n))`.
  - Under (a) it needs its holder class by name, `Class.forName(n + "$RTTIc", …)` and a reflective read of `ONLY`. That is one more class for every distinct number, besides the stamped class that every new size of a generic needs under either variant.
- **Who can make the descriptor.** Under (a) only the Fortress loader can make a holder class. A class defined by any other loader that names `<n>$RTTIc` would fail to link, as the control does (`r1-descriptor.txt:43-45`). None of the nine programs has such a class: E ran them all. Under (b) there is no class to find.
- **The names in the loader.** Under (a) a new kind of class name, starting with a digit, enters the loader's name tests. Under (b) none does.
- **Per call.** At the dispatcher's literal leaf, (a) reads a static final field on every dispatched call through the arm, and (b) calls `RTTIsize.of` and looks the text up in a hash table. Only an arm that is generic and also names a literal size inside its parameter type has this leaf, such as `h[\T\](v: Vec[\T,3\])`. Arms with only literal sizes are tested by `instanceof` on the stamped class under both (`size-cost.md` § 4). No program here loops over such an arm, so the difference was not measured. If it shows, the dispatcher's class could fetch the literal's descriptor once into a static field.
- **Code.** (a) is one file and leaves the compiler alone. (b) is four files and changes what the compiler emits at two sites.

The worker's reading, not a decision: name (b) in the rung's brief.

1. A size made at run time, which the array rung will need, goes through `RTTIsize.of` directly. Under (a) it needs a class per number and a lookup by name.
2. It keeps digit-named classes out of the loader, and the one-object-per-number property does not depend on which loader defined a class.
3. On everything measured here the two are equal: same answers, same descriptor, same hash defect with the same one-method fix, and a footprint within about a kilobyte.

Against (b): four files instead of one; about 120 bytes more in each stamped class that names a literal; a table lookup per dispatched call through a literal leaf, unmeasured.

In the rule's bracket in § 9 of the design brief, the words for (b) are "by a factory on `RTTIsize` from the literal, with `MethodInstantiater.rttiReference`, the extends-clause push and the dispatcher's literal leaf calling it instead of reading `<n>$RTTIc.ONLY`". The second stop condition there, "a number's descriptor needs anything but the literal's text", is not met by either variant: both make it from the text alone.

## 4. Operator arguments, and the instantiations that differ only in them

- The specification's algebra needs one type to be several instantiations of one generic that differ only in an operator argument: `Boolean` extends eight `BooleanAlgebra[\Boolean,...\]` (`basic-lib/booleans.tex:18-36`); ℤ six `CommutativeRing[\ZZ,...\]`; a ring is a `Monoid` at `+` and at `TIMES`. If operator arguments counted, the algebra chapter could not be written, and route A never decided that.
- The specification makes an operator argument a name: the subtrait "inherits methods whose names are the actual operator names instead of the operator parameter names", and any declarations of the actual operator "are irrelevant to the behavior of the operator parameter" (`basic/trait-parameters.tex:224-229`).
- The rule's reason needs the run time to tell instantiations apart: a specialised generic overload picked by the value's type for a caller promised another instantiation. On both paths an operator argument is a compile-time name, its descriptor slot is null, and "no site on either path dispatches on, compares or type-tests an operator argument" (FACTS 2026-09-24, `perf-probes/nat/opr-kind-history.md`). So the unsoundness the rule guards against cannot arise from operator arguments.
- The checker agrees: `checkP` compares type arguments and returns "no exclusion" for any other kind of argument (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:460-463`, `//Todo: Handle int, nat, bool args`, `case _ => pFalse()`). The compiled path refuses `OprInstancesOplus` for an unrelated reason, the same one that refuses a single instantiation (`OprSingle`: "The inherited abstract method ODOT ... has no concrete implementation"); walk runs both (`7`, `12`).

**Judgement.** Operator arguments do not make two instantiations distinct for the rule, and the revised specification says so in the rule's sentence. This agrees with the gatherer's reading, on the grounds above rather than on the implementation alone. The team's later chapter leaves the question where it was: its sentence makes instantiations exclude when the arguments of a non-covariant parameter "are not type equivalent" (`types.tick:357-360`), a relation it defines for types and not for operators, and the restart has no algebra chapter to test the sentence against.

## 5. Where the revised specification states the rule

- Once, as a property of the exclusion relation, in `basic/types-vals-vars.tex` beside the other properties (`:210-216`, the excludes clause, arrow and tuple types, `()` and `BottomType`): two instantiations of one generic trait exclude each other unless every static argument other than an operator argument is the same. The name: "instantiation exclusion", the team's later short form, with "multiple instantiation exclusion" and the 2011 paper cited. The section already says the relations "are the smallest ones that satisfy all the properties given in those sections" (`:187-189`), so the new property slots in without changing the definition's form.
- This is where the team put it themselves. Luchangco's later chapter states instantiation exclusion in exactly this place, as which instantiations exclude each other (`types.tick:355-360`), and his note beside it says the section "should say only which instantiations exclude each other, as it does", while the rule proper "is a rule applied to trait declarations" (`:361-376`). The revised text takes that two-part form in his words, restricted to invariant parameters: in the types chapter, the exclusion between instantiations; in the traits chapter, the rule on declarations.
- The declaration rule in his stronger form (`:364-368`): a trait that extends two instantiations of a generic type, directly or indirectly, must extend an expressible instantiation that is a subtype of both. With every parameter invariant, no instantiation is below two different ones, so it reads: a trait or object may not extend two different instantiations of one generic, directly or through its supertraits. That sentence goes into `basic/traits.tex` beside the `InclusiveMolecule` example (`:286-292`), and the checker's message "Parent must not extend them" is that rule.
- Its consequences then follow from sentences the specification already has: no value has a type below two excluding types (`:140-143`); a declaration may not extend two excluding types (`basic/traits.tex:286-292`).
- The where-clause section (`trait-parameters.tex`) states the consequence for where-clause variables in one sentence, a where-clause variable may not appear as a static argument in an `extends` clause, with E1, E2 and E3 as its three "Not allowed" examples and the widening function and `Empty[\T\]` as the ways. Luchangco's note at `basic/traits.tex:174-180` is answered there, by a cross-reference or by replacing the note.
- Whatever S1 decides about the form of a change (`reviews/spec-change-form.md`), the rule's sentence and the counterexamples are body text; the original wording of each example and route C go where S1 puts them. That is the only place S1 and S2 meet.

## 6. Sizes and boolean arguments: one probe

The papers define the rule over "distinct applications of a type constructor" (`exclusion.tick:143-144`), which counts every static argument. Design B, his decision of 2026-09-24, gives a size a run-time descriptor and dispatch tells `Vec[\3\]` from `Vec[\4\]` (FACTS, the size probes entry). So a value that is both would let a size-specialised overload be picked for a caller promised the other size, the rule's own kind of hole. The checker does not compare sizes in the rule (`case _ => pFalse()`). The probe, run for this brief through a copy of `spec-refused-examples/run.sh` pointed at the session's scratchpad, so that nothing was written under the tree:

```
component JSizeDouble
export Executable
trait Vec[\nat n\]
end
object V extends { Vec[\3\], Vec[\4\] }
end
f(x: Vec[\3\]): String = "f took a Vec[3]"
run():() = do
  v: V = V
  println(f(v))
end
end
```

- walk: `f took a Vec[3]`, rc 0.
- compile: no hierarchy error; the checker passed the declaration, and the compile then died in code generation at `CodeGen.java:5793`, `CompilerError: Only emitting RTTI for types right now`, the size-in-extends site the run-time size rung already owns (FACTS 2026-09-26, rung N, `XXXNatOverrideChecker`).

**Judgement.** The rule counts sizes and boolean arguments; the checker's `pFalse` for them is a defect against the rule as stated, and a candidate ledger row (section 9). The team's later sentence reads the same way, since a size parameter is a non-covariant parameter and `3` and `4` are not the same argument (`types.tick:357-360`), with the caveat of section 4 that its "type equivalent" is defined for types. Its repair is a few lines at `checkP` with a gated expected-failure compile test, and its natural home is the run-time size rung's gather, where sizes get their run-time identity. This differs from the gatherer, who would have the specification say "type arguments only, as the implementation does".

## Manifest and scatter (item 8)
